quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-01.title: Conjugation permutes the simple factors
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-01.body:
**(a)** $\mathbf Z(N)$ is characteristic in $N\trianglelefteq G$, so $\mathbf Z(N)\trianglelefteq G$. By minimality $\mathbf Z(N)=1$ or $N$, and $\mathbf Z(N)=N$ would make $N$, hence $S_1$, abelian. So $\mathbf Z(N)=1$. If some $S_i$ were abelian, it would commute with itself and with every $S_j$, $j\ne i$, so $S_i\le\mathbf Z(N)=1$; but simple groups are nontrivial. Hence every $S_i$ is nonabelian.

**(b)** The argument works for any $S_k$ in place of $S_1$. Let $T=S_k^g$. Since $S_k\trianglelefteq N$ and $N^g=N$, $T\trianglelefteq N$, and $T$ is nonabelian simple. For each $j$, $T\cap S_j\trianglelefteq T$ (as $S_j\trianglelefteq N$), so $T\cap S_j\in\{1,T\}$. If $T\cap S_j=1$ for all $j$, then $[T,S_j]\le T\cap S_j=1$ for all $j$ (both normal in $N$), so $T$ centralizes $N$ and $T\le\mathbf Z(N)=1$ — impossible. Thus $T\le S_j$ for some $j$; as $T\trianglelefteq N$, $T\trianglelefteq S_j$, and simplicity of $S_j$ gives $T=S_j$.

**(c)** By (b) (for every $k$), $G$ acts by conjugation on $\Sigma=\{S_1,\dots,S_r\}$; these are $r$ distinct subgroups since the product is direct with nontrivial factors. Let $\mathcal O$ be the orbit of $S_1$ and $M=\prod_{S\in\mathcal O}S$. Conjugation permutes $\mathcal O$, so $M\trianglelefteq G$, and $1\ne M\le N$; by minimality $M=N$. If some $S_j\notin\mathcal O$, then $M$ is contained in the product of the factors other than $S_j$, which meets $S_j$ trivially, contradicting $S_j\le N=M$. So the action is transitive, and by the orbit–stabilizer theorem the stabilizer $\mathbf N_G(S_1)$ has index $|\Sigma|=r$ in $G$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-02.title: Saturation with respect to a prime
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-02.body:
**(a)** Since $1\in M$, $I\subseteq I'$ for every ideal $I$; in particular $I'\subseteq(I')'$. Conversely, let $r\in(I')'$: $rm\in I'$ for some $m\in M$, so $rmm'\in I$ for some $m'\in M$. As $P$ is prime, $mm'\in M$, hence $r\in I'$. So $(I')'=I'$.

$I'=R$ iff $1\in I'$ iff $m=1\cdot m\in I$ for some $m\in M$ iff $I\cap M\ne\emptyset$.

**(b)** If $Q\cap M\ne\emptyset$ then $Q'=R$ by (a). Suppose $Q\cap M=\emptyset$ and let $r\in Q'$, say $rm\in Q$ with $m\in M$. If $r\notin Q$, then since $Q$ is primary some $m^k\in Q$; but $m^k\in M$, contradicting $Q\cap M=\emptyset$. So $r\in Q$ and $Q'=Q$.

$P$ is prime, hence primary, and $P\cap M=\emptyset$; so $P'=P$.

**(c)** The operation is monotone: $I\subseteq J$ implies $I'\subseteq J'$. Hence $I'\subseteq P'=P$, so $I'\neq R$ and $\sqrt{I'}\subseteq P$. Also $I'\supseteq I\supseteq P^n$ gives $\sqrt{I'}\supseteq\sqrt{P^n}=P$. So $\sqrt{I'}=P$.

Now let $ab\in I'$ with $b\notin\sqrt{I'}=P$, i.e. $b\in M$. Then $abm\in I$ for some $m\in M$, and $bm\in M$, so $a\in I'$. This is exactly the statement that $I'$ is primary (if $ab\in I'$ and $a\notin I'$ then $b\in\sqrt{I'}$). ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-03.title: Normal subfields
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-03.body:
**(a)** Let $\alpha\in L$ be a root of $f$. $L/\mathbb Q$ is Galois, and $H=\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q(\alpha))$ is normal in the abelian group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$. By the Galois correspondence, $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ is a Galois, in particular normal, extension of $\mathbb Q$. A normal extension containing one root of the irreducible polynomial $f$ contains all of them, so $f$ splits over $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$; with $f$ irreducible of degree $\ge2$, $f$ is special.

**(b)** By the primitive element theorem $L=\mathbb Q(\gamma)$. Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\gamma$; it is irreducible of degree $[L:\mathbb Q]\ge2$. Since $L/\mathbb Q$ is normal and contains the root $\gamma$, $f$ splits over $L=\mathbb Q(\gamma)$. So $f$ is special with a root in $L$.

**(c)** $f=X^n-2$ is irreducible by Eisenstein at $2$, of degree $n\ge3$. Let $\alpha$ be any root and $\beta=\sqrt[n]2\in\mathbb R$. Since both are roots of the irreducible $f$, there is a $\mathbb Q$-isomorphism $\sigma\colon\mathbb Q(\alpha)\to\mathbb Q(\beta)$. If $f=\prod_i(X-\alpha_i)$ with all $\alpha_i\in\mathbb Q(\alpha)$, applying $\sigma$ to the coefficients (which are rational, hence fixed) gives $f=\prod_i(X-\sigma(\alpha_i))$ with $\sigma(\alpha_i)\in\mathbb Q(\beta)\subseteq\mathbb R$. So all roots of $f$ would be real. But $\beta e^{2\pi i/n}$ is a root, and it is not real for $n\ge3$. Hence $f$ is not special. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-04.title: Gram matrices
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-04.body:
**(a)** Let $v=\sum_ic_i\alpha_i$ with coordinate row vector $c=(c_1,\dots,c_n)$. By linearity $\theta(v,V)=0$ iff $\theta(v,\alpha_j)=0$ for all $j$, and $\theta(v,\alpha_j)=\sum_ic_i\theta(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=(cM_{\mathcal A})_j$. So such $v\ne0$ exists iff $cM_{\mathcal A}=0$ has a nonzero solution $c$, iff $M_{\mathcal A}$ is singular.

**(b)** By bilinearity,
$$\theta(\beta_i,\beta_k)=\sum_{j,l}p_{ij}\,\theta(\alpha_j,\alpha_l)\,p_{kl}=(PM_{\mathcal A}P^T)_{ik},$$
so $M_{\mathcal B}=P\,M_{\mathcal A}\,P^T$.

**(c)** Since $\theta$ is a symmetric positive definite form (an inner product), the Gram–Schmidt process yields a basis $\mathcal B=\{\beta_i\}$ with $\theta(\beta_i,\beta_j)=\delta_{ij}$, i.e. $M_{\mathcal B}=I$. Write $\alpha_i=\sum_jq_{ij}\beta_j$; the matrix $Q=[q_{ij}]$ is nonsingular, being a change-of-basis matrix. Applying (b) with the roles of the bases exchanged,
$$M_{\mathcal A}=Q\,M_{\mathcal B}\,Q^T=QQ^T.$$ ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-05.title: Maximal noetherian submodules
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010f-05.body:
We use: if $X'\subseteq X$ are modules, $X$ is noetherian iff $X'$ and $X/X'$ are; images of noetherian modules are noetherian.

**(a)** Let $N\subsetneq X\subseteq M$.
- If $X/N$ is noetherian then, $N$ being noetherian, $X$ is noetherian, contradicting the maximality of $N$.
- If $X/N$ is artinian, then (being nonzero) it has a minimal nonzero submodule $Y/N$, which is simple and therefore noetherian — impossible by the previous point applied to $Y$.

**(b)** Suppose $M\ne N$ and pick $m\in M\setminus N$. Then $(mR+N)/N$ is a nonzero submodule of $M/N$ and a homomorphic image of $R_R$ (via $r\mapsto mr+N$). If $R$ is right artinian (resp. right noetherian), $R_R$ is artinian (resp. noetherian), and so is its image — contradicting (a). Hence $M=N$ is noetherian.

**(c)** Now $N$ is a right ideal of $R$ maximal among noetherian right ideals. Let $r\in R$. The map $N\to R$, $x\mapsto rx$, is a right $R$-module homomorphism, so its image $rN$ is a right ideal and a noetherian module. Then $N+rN$ is noetherian: $N$ is, and $(N+rN)/N\cong rN/(N\cap rN)$ is an image of $rN$. By maximality $N+rN=N$, i.e. $rN\subseteq N$. So $N$ is also a left ideal, hence a $2$-sided ideal. ∎
